primary_rejection_reason: The Senior Colleague rejects the proposal because mandating urgent external disclosure and interim patient-facing notification could trigger unnecessary alarm or withdrawal of a drug whose omitted subgroup effects may be clinically insignificant, potentially causing more harm than the incremental risk it addresses.

Immediate parallel regulator notification before the independent clinical/statistical review is complete risks triggering labeling changes or market withdrawal on an incomplete evidentiary record, potentially harming current patients if the subgroup signal ultimately proves not robust.

The occupant-protection floor is a hard constraint whose tolerance threshold will be set through political processes without meaningful pedestrian/cyclist input, potentially systematically prioritizing occupant safety over external parties' injury exposure.

The Vehicle Occupant rejected because the 15% occupant-safety floor is relative to a weighting-adjusted baseline that may already disadvantage occupants, failing to guarantee meaningful occupant protection in imminent-unavoidable-collision scenarios.

The pedestrian stakeholder objects that the policy still permits pedestrians or cyclists to face serious-injury probabilities up to the defined worst-case cap (e.g., ~40%), meaning their safety can be legally traded against occupant protection within permissible bounds rather than being consistently prioritized.

The policy's occupant-sacrificing option relies on real-time actuarial harm estimation under severe time constraints, making the predicted harm ratios too unreliable to responsibly trigger an occupant-sacrificing maneuver in imminent-collision scenarios.
